name: Electric shaver (foil/rotary)

lead: An electric shaver cuts hair with moving blades under a perforated foil or rotary head, so the blades do not touch the skin directly. Foil models are often described as closer-cutting; rotary models suit some face shapes and beards better, according to user preference.
It is a grooming tool, and its results last only until hair regrows. Research on skin comfort is mostly from the cosmetic industry.

paras: A motor oscillates or rotates cutters behind a guard; hairs enter holes or slots and are sheared against the guard.
Irritation is possible, and case reports describe contact allergy to nickel or fragrance components in shavers. Skin often needs time to adjust to electric shaving.

lead: An electric shaver, also called an electric razor, is a handheld grooming device in which a motor drives oscillating or rotating blades behind a protective perforated guard, cutting facial or body hair without direct blade contact with the skin.[1] The two main designs are foil shavers, which use a thin perforated foil over oscillating cutters, and rotary shavers, which use rotating cutting heads.[1][2]

Electric shaving is commonly offered as an alternative to blade razors for people who find wet shaving irritating, although published sources describe skin comfort as something manufacturers have had to balance against how closely the device cuts. A 2016 review from the cosmetic science literature describes research aimed at reducing electric-shaving-induced skin irritation.[3]
No randomised clinical trial comparing electric shavers with blade razors for appearance outcomes.
infobox: Mains or rechargeable battery; many models are wet/dry

paras: Foil shavers pass hairs through a thin perforated foil to oscillating cutters beneath; Wikipedia notes they can shave closer to the skin and are often preferred by professional barbers. Rotary shavers use rotating blades across the head.[2] Users tend to favour one type over the other.[2] Grokipedia describes typical motor speeds of 10,000 to 14,000 cycles per minute.[1]

Early models were for dry skin only, while many modern shavers are waterproof or water-resistant and can be used in the shower.[2] Wikipedia also notes that skin often needs time to adjust to how an electric razor lifts and cuts hair, and that moisturisers designed for electric shaving exist.[2]

John Francis O'Rourke filed a US patent for an electric razor in 1898, and Johann Bruecker reportedly built the first working electric razor in 1915.[2] Colonel Jacob Schick patented a design in 1930 and is often called the father of the modern electric razor; Remington Rand began production in 1937.[2] Alexandre Horowitz of Philips designed one of the first rotary shavers, introduced as the Philishave in 1939.[1][2] Battery-powered models appeared in the late 1940s, and Remington introduced the first rechargeable model in 1960.[2] Roland Ullmann of Braun is credited with many patents on dry shavers.[2]

No studies found comparing electric shavers with other methods for appearance outcomes. A 2016 review summarises manufacturer-side research on skin irritation from electric shaving and on design features intended to reduce it.[3]

Case reports describe allergic contact dermatitis linked to a shaver itself: one report assessed nickel release from an electric shaver in a case of allergic nickel dermatitis,[4] and another described facial contact dermatitis from fragrance ingredients released by an electric shaver.[5] These are isolated reports, not estimates of how common such reactions are.
Shaving of any kind can cause irritation, and the 2016 review treats electric-shaving irritation as an area for ongoing design improvement.[3]
No looksmaxxing forum material specific to electric shavers.
